client: Lately, I’ve been having such a hard time focusing at work. Ever since my grandmother passed away, I just feel this heavy sadness that won’t go away, and it’s hard to get through the day without feeling overwhelmed. I’m not sure if therapy can really help with grief—it feels like something I just have to endure.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a deep, quiet sorrow that makes even daily tasks feel overwhelming right now. Grief can feel like something we must simply bear, but therapy can offer ways to process these heavy emotions so they become more manageable with time. Your voice sounds tired and weighed down—would it help to explore what this sadness is making you think about yourself or your ability to cope?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I keep thinking I should be handling this better by now—it's been months. The sadness makes me feel weak, like I'm failing at moving forward. When people say "time heals," it just makes me angry because time feels like it's making everything worse instead.
therapist: Your voice sounds tense and hurried, like this frustration and sadness are pressing heavily on you right now. It’s understandable to feel angry when it seems like time isn’t helping—grief doesn’t follow a timeline, and expecting yourself to “handle it better” can add extra pressure. Let’s explore what “moving forward” means to you and whether those expectations might be adding to the weight you’re carrying.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Moving forward to me means being productive again, not crying randomly at my desk, not feeling like I'm disappointing everyone around me by being this sad. But when I try to push through, it just makes me feel more exhausted and guilty for not being back to "normal." I don't know how to balance grieving and functioning.
therapist: Your voice sounds rushed and strained, like this pressure to be “normal” is weighing heavily on you. It’s so hard to balance grief and daily life, especially when guilt creeps in—but grief isn’t something to push through; it’s something to move *with*. Let’s explore how you might redefine “functioning” in a way that honors your feelings without adding to the exhaustion.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess I’ve never really thought about redefining what functioning looks like—it’s always just been about keeping up with everything, even if I’m struggling. But the idea of moving *with* my grief instead of pushing through it feels really foreign. I’m not sure how to do that without feeling like I’m giving up or letting people down.
therapist: Your voice sounds thoughtful but uncertain, like this idea feels both intriguing and a bit unfamiliar. It’s completely natural to worry about letting others down, but moving with your grief isn’t giving up—it’s creating space for healing in a way that respects your emotions. Could we explore what small steps might feel manageable to you, even if they’re different from what you’ve done before?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Maybe small steps could look like letting myself take short breaks when I feel overwhelmed at work, instead of forcing through it. But I worry that if I start allowing those moments, I'll just fall apart completely—like the sadness will take over if I give it any space at all. It's scary to loosen my grip on keeping it all together.
therapist: Your voice sounds quiet and hesitant, like you're tentatively considering this shift but still carrying real fear about what might happen if you loosen control. It makes sense to worry that sadness could overwhelm you—but what if giving it small, intentional moments of space actually helps it feel *less* consuming over time? You’re not falling apart; you’re learning to navigate this in a way that honors your needs.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I never thought about it that way—that giving sadness space might actually make it feel smaller, not bigger. But it's so hard to trust that process when everything in me wants to tighten up and push through. What if I try taking those breaks and just end up crying in the bathroom stall every time? That doesn't feel like progress.
therapist: Your voice sounds higher and a bit unsteady—like this idea brings both hope and nervousness, especially when you imagine those bathroom breaks turning into uncontrollable tears. But progress isn’t about stopping the sadness; it’s about letting it exist without judgment. What if those moments of crying *are* part of the healing, even if they don’t feel tidy or productive? You’re learning to trust yourself with these emotions, and that’s brave.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I know intellectually that crying is normal, but it still feels like failure to me—like I'm not strong enough to keep it together. The idea that tears could be part of healing just doesn't match how I was raised, where emotions were something to power through. Maybe that's why this whole process feels so uncomfortable.
therapist: Your voice sounds rushed and strained, like this clash between what you know intellectually and what you feel emotionally is really unsettling for you. It’s understandable that this process feels uncomfortable when you were taught to push through emotions—but strength isn’t about keeping it together; it’s about facing these feelings with honesty. Let’s explore how you might begin to redefine what strength looks like for you, even if it feels unfamiliar at first.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Redefining strength feels so foreign—like I’m rewriting a rulebook I’ve followed my whole life. But I also see how keeping it all bottled up hasn’t been helping me. I guess I’m just scared that if I start allowing myself to feel, I’ll lose control completely and never get it back. It’s hard to trust that I won’t drown in it.
therapist: Your voice sounds soft and uncertain, like this idea of redefining strength feels both important and deeply unsettling. It’s understandable to feel scared about losing control—but allowing yourself to feel doesn’t mean drowning; it means learning to swim through these emotions rather than fighting against them. Let’s explore how you might take small, manageable steps toward trusting yourself with this process.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I like the swimming analogy - it makes me feel less afraid of the emotions. But I still don't know where to start with these small steps. Part of me worries that if I try to "swim" through the grief, I'll just sink anyway because I've never learned how to do this before. It's frustrating to feel so clumsy with my own feelings.
therapist: Your voice sounds hesitant but thoughtful, like you’re tentatively considering this new way of approaching grief even though it feels unfamiliar and frustrating. It’s completely normal to feel clumsy with emotions you’ve never let yourself fully experience—but every swimmer starts somewhere, and even small steps can help you build confidence in navigating these feelings. Let’s explore what one tiny, manageable step might look like for you today.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess one tiny step could be letting myself cry for a few minutes when I feel it coming, instead of immediately trying to suppress it. But I’m worried that once I start, I won’t be able to stop—like the floodgates will open and I’ll spiral into uncontrollable sadness. It’s hard to trust that I can keep it contained to just a few minutes.
therapist: Your voice sounds high and hurried—I hear how nervous this idea makes you, like standing at the edge of those floodgates. But emotions often feel less overwhelming when we give them *some* space, rather than none at all. What if we practiced just noticing that initial urge to cry, without judgment, and seeing what happens next together? You might surprise yourself with how much you can manage when you take it moment by moment.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
